name: Cleveland
blurb: Highest yields of any major metro; city-proper price-to-rent ratios run near 10 versus the metro-wide 14. Cleveland Clinic and the universities anchor tenant demand.

name: Toledo
blurb: Cheapest entry among tracked metros with a ratio of 13 and deep sub-$100K single-family stock — a natural first BRRRR market.

name: Pittsburgh
blurb: A ratio of 13 on a stable eds-and-meds economy. Slow appreciation: investors buy the rent check, not the flip.

name: Memphis
blurb: The turnkey capital of America, with the deepest out-of-state investor infrastructure, a ratio of 14, and no state income tax.

name: Birmingham
blurb: Among the highest projected rental yields nationally, paired with the lowest property taxes of any tracked market.

name: Detroit
blurb: The best raw city-level price-to-rent anywhere, with block-by-block risk. Suburbs are the institutional play.

name: Tulsa
blurb: A ratio of 14, landlord-friendly courts, and little coastal capital competing for deals.

name: Oklahoma City
blurb: Low prices on a steady energy-and-aerospace employment base. Underrated and uncrowded.

name: Little Rock
blurb: Cheap entry, low taxes, and quiet competition — a patient operator's market.

name: Indianapolis
blurb: The best blend of cash flow and growth: real population and rent gains, fast evictions, no rent control.

name: Kansas City
blurb: Roughly 123% appreciation over the past decade means equity actually compounds — fuel for the refinance snowball.

name: St. Louis
blurb: Strong rent-to-price ratios with unusually deep duplex and fourplex stock for stacking doors.

name: New Orleans
blurb: A ratio of 14 that shrinks fast once insurance quotes arrive — premiums can consume 100+ basis points of yield.

name: San Antonio
blurb: A ratio of 16 with no state income tax, offset partly by 2%+ effective property taxes.

name: Huntsville
blurb: Cash flow with a genuine defense-and-aerospace growth engine and high tenant quality; concentration is the tradeoff.

name: Chicago
blurb: A ratio of 13 undercut by 2%+ property taxes and slow, tenant-tilted courts. Yield you cannot collect is not yield.

name: Austin
blurb: A ratio of 21 and gross yield under 5% — a reference market showing where the snowball math stops working.

name: Denver
blurb: A ratio of 25 means negative leverage at 2026 mortgage rates — a rent-lean reference market.
